title: Wolf-Rayet star, WR 134
caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 134 and its blue arc, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: The brightest star below the center of this image is WR 134, and in the upper left curves a blue arc of gas. WR 134 is a Wolf-Rayet star, a very hot, massive star that is shedding its outer layers.

Those layers stream away from the star at very high speeds. Part of the ejected material shows up as the blue arc, which formed where the star's outer layer slammed into the nebula already surrounding it.

Massive stars live fast and short lives, and they return large amounts of material to space. Structures like this arc show that process in action, as outflowing gas sweeps up and shapes the clouds that surround the star, long before it reaches the end of its life.

understand.summary: The Mayall 4-meter Telescope's Mosaic camera used two narrowband filters. Hydrogen-alpha is shown in red and sulfur [S II] in blue.
filters: 672 nm · Optical Sll (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
656 nm · Optical Ha (NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope Mosaic I)
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate faint light from individual gases, revealing an arc the eye could not see.
